description: Explains every canonical CNA C API function CNA-Java does not bind, in two independent fields. `classification` and `purposeReason` answer why the route exists for CNA-Java; `bindingStatus`, `bindingReason` and `evidence` answer the separate question of why it is not bound. Rules are ordered and the first match wins. A bound function is never matched here: its classification is derived from the Java packages that actually reach it.

classifications.XNA_BACKING: Derived only. A bound route reached from the strict Microsoft.Xna.Framework projection.
classifications.CNA_EXTENSION_CANDIDATE: A CNA capability outside XNA 4.0. It belongs under org.openeggbert.cna.extensions, whether or not it is bound yet.
classifications.JAVA_INTERNAL_ONLY: Derived only. A bound route reached only from org.openeggbert.cna.internal plumbing.
classifications.NOT_USEFUL_IN_JAVA: A route CNA-Java must not take, because Java already owns the behaviour or the route has no Java meaning.
classifications.DEFERRED_RUNTIME: An XNA-backing route that is not bound yet. A backlog task owns it.
classifications.UNMAPPED_REQUIRES_REVIEW: Default when no rule matches. The coverage gate fails on it.

rules.purposeReason: The mutators of NetworkSessionProperties, which XNA declares as a fixed list of eight slots.
rules.bindingReason: XNA's Add, Insert, Remove, RemoveAt and Clear throw NotSupportedException because the list has a fixed size, and CNA now enforces the same (GS-007b). Java answers UnsupportedOperationException itself; binding a route that can only refuse would add a boundary without behaviour.
rules.evidence: Re-measured 2026-09-30 against ABI 0.35.0: a new NetworkSessionProperties reports eight unset slots; NetworkSessionNativeIntegrationTests asserts the size, the round trip through set, and the refusals.

rules.purposeReason: Vector2/3/4 arithmetic is managed in XNA and managed in CNA-Java. Routing each operation through JNI would add a per-call cost and a native failure mode the original managed API cannot produce.
rules.bindingReason: Routing a pure value operation through JNI would add a per-call cost and a native failure mode the original managed API cannot produce, for a result the Java value type already computes to the same specified bits.

rules.purposeReason: GameComponent, DrawableGameComponent, GameComponentCollection and the service container are managed XNA behaviour. CNA-Java owns the component list and the Java Game drives it, so a parallel native component list would be a second source of truth.
rules.bindingReason: CNA-Java owns the component list and the Java Game drives it. A parallel native component list would be a second source of truth for the same update order, and the two would drift the first time either side added a component.

rules.purposeReason: Lends a fresh name for something the caller gave the lender, and a fresh name is a game child: measured in lent_effect_lifetime.c, taking one of these twice and releasing neither makes cna_game_destroy answer INVALID_STATE, and releasing both makes the same run answer SUCCESS. So a Java getter over one of these would allocate and free a native handle on every read, to hand back an object the Java facade already retains -- Skybox, ColorGradePass, PostProcessPass, ClusteredForwardEffect and RenderPipeline each keep what they were given and answer from that. The same reasoning as PbrMaterialExtensions' nine texture getters.
rules.bindingReason: A Java getter over one of these would allocate and free a native handle on every read to hand back an object the Java facade already retains, and a leaked one makes the game undestroyable.
rules.evidence: lent_effect_lifetime.c: taking one twice and releasing neither makes cna_game_destroy answer INVALID_STATE; releasing both makes the same run answer SUCCESS.

rules.purposeReason: Lends back the identical handle the caller gave cna_render_pipeline_set_skybox -- measured, not assumed: unlike the six fresh-name getters beside it this one is the same name, so there is nothing to release and nothing a Java facade could add. RenderPipeline answers from the Skybox it was handed.
rules.bindingReason: It lends back the identical handle the caller passed in, so a Java facade could add nothing to the Skybox it already holds.
rules.evidence: lent_effect_lifetime.c: the returned handle compares equal to the one given to cna_render_pipeline_set_skybox, unlike the six fresh-name getters beside it.

rules.purposeReason: Fills a caller-provided struct with invalid handles and its struct_size/struct_version. The generated JNI adapter already writes both fields for every route that consumes these structs, as sizeof against the live header and the header's own declared version -- a compile-time value that breaks the build when the header changes, where the runtime route would absorb the change silently. CNA_INVALID_HANDLE is zero, which a fresh Java array already is.
rules.bindingReason: The generated adapter already writes struct_size and struct_version for every route that consumes these structs, from sizeof against the live header and the header's own declared version, and CNA_INVALID_HANDLE is zero, which a fresh Java array already is.
rules.evidence: A compile-time value breaks the build when the header changes; this runtime route would absorb the same change silently.

rules.purposeReason: A pure bitmask containment test over two integers the caller supplies, which java.util.EnumSet answers without crossing JNI. CNA's own bit values are pinned in probe.c by compile-time assertion against the live header, which is stronger than any runtime route could be.
rules.bindingReason: java.util.EnumSet answers a bitmask containment test over two caller-supplied integers without crossing JNI.
rules.evidence: probe.c pins CNA's own bit values by compile-time assertion against the live header, which is stronger than any runtime route could be.

rules.purposeReason: Fills a CNA_PbrMaterialEXT with its documented defaults and its size and version headers; the material itself is a CNA extension with no XNA 4.0 counterpart.
rules.bindingReason: The generated adapter already writes struct_size and struct_version for every route that consumes this structure, from sizeof against the live header and the header's own declared version -- a compile-time value that breaks the build when the header changes, where this runtime route would absorb the same change silently. The remaining defaults are what PbrMaterialExt's own Java constructor sets, and a Java record is where a default belongs when the caller is Java.
rules.evidence: The same decision the two glTF material struct initialisers already carry, and the same argument: a compile-time size is stronger than a runtime one.

rules.purposeReason: The extended graphics layer -- render pipeline settings, tone mapping, render and shadow quality, ASCII/CRT/dither post-process identities -- is explicitly beyond XNA 4.0.
rules.bindingReason: Nothing is left unbound here; the rule exists so a new graphics_ext.h declaration is classified rather than unexplained.

rules.purposeReason: Reports the renderer this build was compiled with -- CNA documents it as the compiled-in renderer, which on a multi-renderer build is the default rather than the one chosen. GraphicsRenderer.getActive() answers which renderer is running, and CnaRuntime already projects the compiled-in renderer through its name route.
rules.bindingReason: Its answer is already reachable twice: getActive() for the running renderer and CnaRuntime's name route for the compiled-in one. A third route named 'current' would only invite reading it as the running renderer.
rules.evidence: core_ext.h documents cna_graphics_renderer_copy_current_name and its type sibling as the compiled-in renderer (getCurrentGraphicsRendererType is a compile-time constant). JAVA-UPSTREAM-018, which once blocked this family, was a probe artifact and is withdrawn.

rules.purposeReason: A per-level alias for cna_logger_log(level, message, category), which is bound and which CnaLogger routes every level through. Binding seven more entry points that differ only in a constant would widen the native boundary without widening what a game can do.
rules.bindingReason: Seven more entry points that differ from the bound cna_logger_log only by a constant would widen the native boundary without widening what a game can do; CnaLogger routes every level through the one that is bound.

rules.purposeReason: Emits only when a condition holds, and takes no category -- so it is not a conditional form of the route beside it. `if (condition) CnaLogger.Info(message, category)` is the same behaviour with the category kept and without crossing JNI when the condition is false, which is the case these exist for.
rules.bindingReason: These take no category, so they are not a conditional form of the route beside them. `if (condition) CnaLogger.Info(message, category)` is the same behaviour with the category kept and without crossing JNI when the condition is false, which is the case they exist for.

rules.purposeReason: Installs the hook CNA calls when a sensor is disposed, so its own tests can watch a teardown they cannot otherwise observe.
rules.bindingReason: The one sensor callback with no registration to release: it is cleared by passing null or by the sensor going away, so a Java handler would be pinned for the sensor's whole life with no deterministic release point a caller could reach. What it observes is CNA's own disposal ordering, which a Java caller already knows -- it is the caller that called dispose.
rules.evidence: SensorInjectionTests exercises the disposal path directly instead: dispose stops the sensor, every route on it then answers INVALID_STATE, and a second dispose is refused.

rules.purposeReason: Constructing, comparing, hashing and printing the description CNA's obsolete reading-changed event carries instead of a reading.
rules.bindingReason: AccelerometerReading is a Java record, and the obsolete event is projected onto it rather than onto a second value type: the description holds one reading's three axes and a timestamp, which is what the record already is. Construction, equality, hashing and toString are the language's and are exact.

rules.purposeReason: Constructing, comparing, hashing and printing an accelerometer sample.
rules.bindingReason: Every reading here is a Java record, so its construction, equality, hashing and string form are the language's and are exact. A native constructor would be a second way to build a value the sensor already hands over complete, and a native equality a second definition of the one the record generates. This is the rule the whole input and vector value-type families already carry, and the readings are flattened into and out of CNA's own structures where it matters -- which is what the injection tests assert field by field.

rules.purposeReason: Places text on the host clipboard, which XNA 4.0 has no counterpart for.
rules.bindingReason: cna_devices_clipboard_set_text_ext is the same operation with the platform's answer attached, and Clipboard.SetText returns it. This form deliberately reports nothing, reproducing a canonical method that returns void; binding both would give a game two ways to make the same request and one of them would silently discard whether the host took it.

rules.purposeReason: A CNA test seam that clears the enumerated device tables.
rules.bindingReason: Exposing it would let a consumer change what the device-enumeration surface reports, which is the opposite of what that surface is for -- the same rule the mouse and gamer test seams already carry. The hot-plug raise routes beside it are bound because they add an event a game can observe rather than removing state it can read.

rules.purposeReason: CNA's process-wide table mapping a .cnb asset type identifier to the code that turns such a file into a runtime object. The .cnb container has no XNA 4.0 counterpart.
rules.bindingReason: Two of these decide it and cnb.h says both outright. register takes a CNA_CnbLoaderCallback and a context that "must outlive the registration, which is process-wide"; invoke returns the loaded object through a void** and the header states that "only a loader registered from C produces something C can hold". A Java loader returns a Java object: there is no pointer to give CNA and none to receive back, so the void** is not an obstacle to work around but the boundary saying this table is for C loaders. find calls itself "the wrong entry point for loading a file" and resolve produces a loader only C can call; clear and remove withdraw a registration Java never made, and destroy releases a loader handle nothing here obtains.
rules.evidence: docs/cnb-loader-registry-decision.md, JAVA-EXT-003. What is worth keeping from CNA's registry is its identity rule rather than its storage, and CnbLoaders implements all three parts of it in Java: a built-in type's number is authoritative, a custom one's is a 31-bit name hash and must be confirmed against the file's canonical name, and a second registration under one identifier with a different name is refused. isRegisteredWithCna and getCnaRegisteredTypeName do reach CNA's own table, because "can the native side read this?" is a real question Java cannot answer for itself.

rules.purposeReason: Picks the first stored texture representation a caller's own predicate accepts, so a game can choose between the compressed forms one .cnb texture carries.
rules.bindingReason: It takes a CNA_CnbTextureFormatSupportedFn, a C function pointer called once per representation inside the call -- and the loop it saves is three lines of Java over getRepresentationCount and getRepresentationFormat, which are bound. A trampoline that crossed into Java once per candidate format would add a callback barrier to a search a caller can run itself, over data it already has.
rules.evidence: CnbTextureData exposes the representation count and each one's format, which is every input the predicate would be given.

rules.purposeReason: The .cnb container, its schemas, its writers and its loader registry are a CNA content format with no XNA 4.0 counterpart.
rules.bindingReason: Nothing is left unbound here beyond the loader registry and the format predicate above; this catch-all exists so a new cnb.h declaration is classified rather than unexplained.

rules.purposeReason: Remaining adapter, display-mode and presentation routes behind the bound GraphicsAdapter and PresentationParameters surface.
rules.bindingReason: An XNA-backing route the named backlog task owns. The Java member it would back is projected and behaves; what is deferred is moving its implementation onto this native route.

rules.purposeReason: XNA's PacketWriter is a BinaryWriter over a growable buffer and its PacketReader is a BinaryReader over the received bytes, and the Java projection is the same. Keeping the buffer managed is what gives Position and Length exactly XNA's meaning over one cursor; a native cursor beside the Java one would be two positions to keep in step, and the packet already crosses the boundary once, at Send and Receive.
rules.bindingReason: Keeping the buffer managed is what gives Position and Length exactly XNA's meaning over one cursor. A native cursor beside the Java one would be two positions to keep in step, and the packet already crosses the boundary once, at Send and Receive.

rules.purposeReason: The asynchronous half of an operation the projection takes synchronously. XNA's Begin/End pair is projected over CNA's synchronous route plus CompletedAsyncResult, because CNA's asynchronous form completes before its own begin route returns; binding both would be two spellings of one operation and two places for its behaviour to drift.

rules.purposeReason: Mutating a collection XNA declares read-only, or asking whether it is. The Java collection throws from every one of those members exactly as XNA's does, so no call site can exist for the native route; and a copy-out is answered from the same snapshot get and size already read.

rules.purposeReason: A CLR enumerator's own lifecycle. Java's Iterator has no reset and its collections iterate by index over the same elements, so projecting a second cursor would add a handle to own and a state to keep in step for no behaviour a Java caller can reach.

rules.purposeReason: A factory for an object the projection receives rather than makes, and the matching release. A gamer, a machine, a friend, an achievement and a session listing all arrive from the roster or the session that owns them, so Java never owns one to free -- and a second owner freeing a borrowed handle is the failure this classification prevents. The handles Java does own are released: JAVA-NATIVE-024 records the three that were not.

The inherited AbstractList walk stays, and it is correct.

rules.purposeReason: Declaring a reflectively serialized .xnb type's field list from outside the runtime is a CNA extension point: it lets a caller read a type the stock content pipeline has no reader for.
rules.bindingReason: The object it fills is a C structure and the declaration is a list of byte offsets into it, which no Java object has. A projection would have to hand CNA the address of a direct ByteBuffer and decode fields back out by offset -- the raw-memory surface this binding's ownership rules exist to keep out of a game's hands. Two further facts settle it rather than leaving it a matter of taste. The create callback's context must outlive a registration that CNA states has no undo -- "the canonical Register() has no undo either" -- so every registered type would pin a Java reference that nothing can ever release. And the Java projection already has the capability by a safer road: org.openeggbert.cna.content.ContentTypeReaderRegistry registers a real ContentTypeReader written in Java, with fields rather than offsets, for the managed reader the strict ContentManager uses.
rules.evidence: content_readers.h: add_field takes an offset_in_bytes, create_callback's context "must outlive the registration", and register has no withdrawal route by design. CNA's own fixture in modules/c-api/tests/pure_c/ContentSmoke.c declares a two-field C struct and passes offsetof for each field. CnaObjectDictionaryTests loads the same fixture without the two entries that need it, which is the TrianglePickingSample shape the family exists for.

rules.purposeReason: XNA's input value types -- GamePadState and its four component structs, KeyboardState, MouseState, TouchLocation, TouchCollection, GestureSample and TouchPanelCapabilities -- are managed structs in XNA and managed values in CNA-Java. Their construction, equality, hashing, string form and indexing are pure value operations with an exactly specified result, so routing them through JNI would add a per-call cost and a native failure mode the original managed API cannot produce. This is the same rule the vector and matrix families carry.
rules.bindingReason: Routing a pure value operation through JNI would add a per-call cost and a native failure mode the original managed API cannot produce, for a result the Java value type already computes to the same specified bits.

bindingStatuses.ACTIONABLE_LOCAL: Nothing outside this repository blocks it. It is work, not a boundary.
bindingStatuses.BLOCKED_UPSTREAM: A reproduced defect or a missing door in CNA or Sharp Runtime blocks it.
bindingStatuses.BLOCKED_RENDERER: No renderer this build can select provides the capability.
bindingStatuses.BLOCKED_HARDWARE: The host has no such device and CNA offers no test or synthetic backend for it.
bindingStatuses.BLOCKED_PLATFORM: The platform CNA is built for does not implement it.
bindingStatuses.DELIBERATE_NON_BINDING: Measured and decided against: binding it would add a boundary without adding behaviour a consumer can reach, or would make an existing guarantee weaker.
bindingStatuses.DEFERRED_TRACKED: An XNA-backing route a named backlog task owns. Only a DEFERRED_RUNTIME rule carrying a task may use it, which is what keeps it from becoming a synonym for 'not looked at'.
